To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sleep and wake affect astrocytes in the mouse brain, and that the effects of sleep on astrocytes are opposite to those of wake.

(1) sleep and wake differentially affect gene expression in astrocytes; (2) wake increases the proximity of astrocytic processes to synapses; and (3) sleep restriction increases the available astrogytic surface in the synapse.
(i) sleep and wake strongly modulate astrocytic gene and ultrastructure, (ii) wake increases astrocytic coverage, and (iii) sleep decreases astrocytic coverage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of sleep/wake on the brain, and how astrocytes may mediate these changes.
the role that astrocytes play in the regulation of brain function and the effects that sleep and wake have on their structure and function.
the astrocytic contribution to the regulation of sleep and wake, and with the astrocyte-dependent modulation of synaptic function as a function of state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
astrocytes undergo state-dependent morphological changes and that these are likely to be functionally significant.
the effects of sleep/wake state are not limited to neuronal activity, but are also relevant for astrocytes.
astrocytes are affected by sleep and wake, and this may have important functional consequences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
astrocytes are highly sensitive to sleep and wake states, and that these states are associated with specific changes in their transcriptome and ultrastructure.
sleep is a state of astrocytic rest, while wake is a state of increased astrocyte activation.
astrocytes are highly sensitive to the sleep/wake states and that their morphology and molecular composition are strongly affected by sleep and wake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sleep and wake are not only a state-dependent switch for neuronal function, but also for astrocyte function.
the brain is not a static organ, but rather a dynamic one, where the astrocytic compartment is constantly adapting to the sleep and wake cycle.
astrocytes are not a static cellular background, but rather an integral part of brain plasticity and homeostasis, and are likely to contribute to the effects of sleep on neuronal function.
